# Practitioner Academy Proposal

**Prepared for:** Dana Whitfield, General Counsel, Tamarack Instruments (fictional)
**Program:** Practitioner Academy, AI Governance Academy
**Format:** Two days, live virtual, four 90-minute working sessions per day
**Price:** US$12,500

## 1. Situation Summary

Tamarack Instruments designs and manufactures laboratory measurement instruments. It is headquartered in the Netherlands, operates in the Netherlands, Germany and the United States, and has about 1,100 staff. The Client's AI portfolio is at three stages:

* **Deployed:** a customer service chatbot on the support portal.
* **Piloting:** AI visual inspection on the German production line.
* **Planned:** AI sales forecasting next year.

The Client's AI maturity is piloting. The regulatory drivers named are the EU AI Act and GDPR. ISO/IEC 42001 work is expected to start next year, and that start date is not fixed.

Three facts shape this proposal:

* An internal audit finding in June 2026 recorded that the Client has no inventory of AI systems.
* Dana Whitfield stated the objective: "I want governance in place before visual inspection goes into production in Q2 2027."
* Three constraints apply. Budget is approved up to US$80,000 this fiscal year. Customer data must stay in the EU. The German works council is consulted before anything touches production staff.

## 2. Why Practitioner Capability Fits the Client Now

The Q2 2027 objective and the audit finding point to the same need: people inside the Client who can build and maintain governance artifacts themselves.

Over two days, the practitioner audience works directly in two repositories:

* GRC Workbook (https://github.com/rolldabones/grc-workbook)
* Slow AI Kitchen (https://github.com/rolldabones/slow-ai-kitchen)

The audience roles are General Counsel, CISO, Head of Quality, Head of Data, German plant manager and two internal auditors. Participants leave with started artifacts and the knowledge of where each one lives.

The program also connects to two references:

* AI Governance for Boards (https://github.com/rolldabones/ai-governance-for-boards) at the board layer.
* The Definition of Done (https://github.com/rolldabones/definition-of-done) at the acceptance layer.

The Profile Block lists an ISO/IEC 27001 ISMS, an ISO 9001 quality management system and an internal audit function. This proposal makes no assumption about the registers, processes, controls or records these hold. Participants may bring relevant documents to map against during the sessions.

The program is taught through three principles: Slow AI, Informed Intent, Final Liability rests with the Human.

## 3. Running Worked Examples

Two use cases serve as the worked examples across both days.

* **AI visual inspection (piloting).** It is tied directly to the stated Q2 2027 objective. It also brings the works council constraint and the EU AI Act into the room.
* **Customer service chatbot (deployed).** It is the system already in use. It allows the customer data residency constraint and GDPR to be worked through in a governed workflow.

AI sales forecasting is used only in the inventory and classification session, so that the started inventory covers all three named systems.

**Data handling.** All exercise material is sanitized. Chatbot exercises use synthetic support interactions containing no customer data. Visual inspection exercises use a synthetic description of an inspection flow, and no exercise uses data about or involving production staff.

## 4. Curriculum Spine and Exercises

### Day 1: Doctrine and GRC Workbook

| Session | Exercise | Repository asset | Artifact produced |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | *The Turtle and the Phoenix*: telling, principles, handle map as the bridge to the workbook modules, then the twenty-minute closing exercise | Facilitation kit (https://github.com/rolldabones/AI-Governance-Academy/blob/main/the-turtle-and-the-phoenix.md): the story, the handle map and section 8 closing exercise | The three artifacts specified in section 8 of the kit |
| 2 | Governance structures: draft decision rights and escalation paths for the visual inspection pilot and the chatbot. Owner fields are left for the Client to assign. | GRC Workbook module: governance structures, with board-layer escalation referenced to AI Governance for Boards | Draft governance structure and escalation map for both worked examples |
| 3 | AI system inventory and classification: record all three use cases and draft EU AI Act classification rationale, flagged for review by counsel | GRC Workbook module: AI system inventories and classification | Started AI system inventory (three entries) with draft classification rationale |
| 4 | Risk and impact assessment and operating procedure: assess both worked examples, then outline an operating procedure that includes a works council consultation check and an EU data residency check | GRC Workbook modules: risk and impact assessments; policies and operating procedures | Draft risk register entries for both worked examples; draft operating procedure outline |

### Day 2: Slow AI Kitchen and Assurance

| Session | Exercise | Repository asset | Artifact produced |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | Governed prompting: write a governed prompt specification for the support chatbot using synthetic interactions | Slow AI Kitchen pattern: governed prompting | Governed prompt specification for the chatbot |
| 6 | Workflow design: build two governed workflows, one for chatbot escalation and one for review of inspection results in a sanitized analog of the pilot. The inspection workflow includes a gate to confirm works council consultation before anything touches production staff. | Slow AI Kitchen pattern: practical AI workflow design | Two governed workflows |
| 7 | Human oversight and accountability: place oversight points and accountable roles on both workflows under the principle Final Liability rests with the Human | Slow AI Kitchen pattern: human oversight and accountability | Oversight and accountability map for both workflows |
| 8 | Evidence and audit readiness: define the evidence each workflow must produce and its acceptance criteria | Slow AI Kitchen pattern: evidence collection and audit readiness, with acceptance criteria drawn from The Definition of Done | Evidence plan and acceptance criteria for both workflows |

## 5. Deliverables

By the close of Day 2, the Client holds the following artifacts in the repositories:

* The three section 8 artifacts from the fable session.
* A started AI system inventory covering the chatbot, visual inspection and sales forecasting.
* Draft risk register entries for the two worked examples.
* A draft operating procedure outline.
* A governed prompt specification.
* At least two governed workflows, each with oversight points, an evidence plan and acceptance criteria.

The Client assigns who owns finishing each artifact; those owners are Unknown at this stage.

**Scope of these deliverables:**

* The artifacts are structured to inform later ISO/IEC 42001 work.
* The program does not promise any certification or audit outcome.
* Draft EU AI Act classifications remain drafts until reviewed by counsel.

## 6. Logistics and Price

**Format.** Two days, live virtual. Each day runs four 90-minute working sessions. Program dates and participant count are Unknown and will be confirmed with the Client.

**Price.** US$12,500. This sits within the stated budget approval of up to US$80,000 this fiscal year.

**Pre-work.** Participants bring three things:

* A list of AI systems in their area.
* Existing policies relevant to AI.
* One live workflow they want governed.

All pre-work materials must be prepared within the Client's confidentiality constraints.

## 7. Next Step

A decision is expected by 15 December 2026. We propose a 30-minute call with Dana Whitfield to cover three points:

1. Confirm program dates.
2. Confirm the participant list against the audience roles.
3. Agree the sanitized analog materials for the two worked examples.

Human-made, for Easy Work, Simply Done.
